newsitem.title: USA: U.S. experts see bumpy ride for Ecuador's reforms.
newsitem.headline: U.S. experts see bumpy ride for Ecuador's reforms.

text.p: Stiff opposition from the Ecuadoran Congress and the country's unions could hamper proposed reforms and even quash the economic plan outlined by President Abdala Bucaram in early December, emerging market debt experts warned.

"I am very concerned about Ecuador. I think we are due to get some important setbacks in the reform process. I think the whole economic plan is in jeopardy," said Walter Molano, director of economic and financial research for Latin America at SBC Warburg in New York.

Experts said they believe the convertibility plan could be defeated later this month by the Social Christians, the main opposition party in the Ecuadoran Congress. The plan, which would peg the currency at four sucres to the dollar, is a key component of Bucaram's economic package.
"Unless he has the support of a broad coalition in the government, Bucaram is not going to be able to implement these type of changes," said Molano.
Masha Shatalina, emerging market research analyst at Morgan Stanley & Co., said Bucaram's plan faces major resistance from opposition parties.
Bucaram opponents last week signed an agreement saying they would block everything the government proposed.
"That is the first time any such agreement had been made, so I see a major risk the convertibility plan will not go through," Shatalina said.

Shatalina said there is still a chance of it passing if it just goes through the plenary. But she said there is an increased risk of it not passing if the President of the Congress calls full Congress.

Even though Bucaram appears fully committed to implementing the convertibility plan, sources said his reversal last week on a fiscal measure regarding the domestic price of cooking gas sounded alarm bells on his commitment to fiscal austerity.

"If the president himself turns around and contradicts and actually reverses a reform that is recognized as being really important for balancing a fiscal account, I think it is cause for concern in terms of his commitment to his own program," said William Romary, senior economist for Latin America at UBS Securities in New York.

Shortly after Ecuador's Energy Minister Alfredo Adum announced that the domestic price of cooking gas would be raised to $4.10 per bottle last week, Bucaram reversed that decision and said the price would only be raised to $2.70.
Romary explained that credible fiscal discipline is very important in any convertibility scenario because the government would have to rely on the capital markets to finance any fiscal deficit.

"We are assuming that the convertibility will not go in on schedule and that has been our forecast all along. There are just so many obstables to it that it will keep getting delayed," the UBS economist said.

Although Bucaram said he would call a referendum if Congress did not pass the economic plan, sources said the Ecuadoran President could face a political embarrassment because he would likely fail to get the neccessary support for a plan that would further slash popular public services.
Indeed, many emerging market experts agreed that Bucaram's party appeared to be losing momentum, given the recent protests against his tough economic reforms.
In Quito on Tuesday, student protests against increases in the cost of public services ended in violence as police fired tear gas at the demonstrators.
Meanwhile, Ecuadoran unions said Monday that they were considering a general strike on February 5 against Bucaram's economic reforms, which include cutting subsidies to public services.

"It's like they are sensing blood in the water and so the sharks could go into a feeding frenzy and I don't think the markets have priced this in at all," said Molano, who expects a sharp correction in Ecuadoran Brady bonds. "I think the markets will end their love affair with Ecuador."
Since December 31, Ecuadoran PDI bonds ECPDI=RR have risen 2-3/4 to 64-1/4 bid from 61-1/2.
